title: Get started
text: This tutorial runs a ready-made design, inspects the known effects, and then builds a second design from reusable components. The full page runs in a few seconds.

title: Get started
text:
1 Install and import
uv add "pypanelsim @ git+https://github.com/apoorvalal/pypanelsim.git"


Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from pypanelsim import core, designs, primitives


The three modules have distinct jobs:

core contains the simulator, results, and random-stream tools.
primitives contains reusable feature, assignment, outcome, and effect models.
designs contains ready-made simulation designs.

section: 5 Compose two-way fixed effects and factors
text:
5 Compose two-way fixed effects and factors
Two-way fixed effects and low-rank factors are reusable outcome models. Combine them with SumOutcomeModel.


Code
outcome_model = primitives.SumOutcomeModel(
    models=(
        primitives.TwoWayFixedEffectsOutcome(
            unit_effect_scale=1.0,
            time_effect_scale=0.5,
            noise_scale=0.2,
        ),
        primitives.LowRankFactorOutcome(
            rank=2,
            loading_scale=1.0,
            factor_scale=0.7,
        ),
    ),
    weights=(1.0, 1.0),
)

simulator = core.PanelSimulator(
    name="fixed_effects_plus_factors",
    dimensions=core.PanelDimensions(n_units=200, n_periods=40),
    assignment=primitives.RandomizedSingleCohortAssignment(
        n_treated=80,
        adoption_period=25,
    ),
    outcome_model=outcome_model,
    effect_model=primitives.LinearRampEffect(slope=0.2),
)

composed_panel = simulator.simulate(seed=17)
print(composed_panel.metadata["outcome"]["model"])
print(round(composed_panel.true_att, 3))

section: 9 Apply the package with PyFixest and crabbymetrics
text:
9 Apply the package with PyFixest and crabbymetrics
pypanelsim does not require an estimator package. Install the optional packages to run this section:
uv sync --extra docs --extra estimators
We compare two panels with the same randomized cohort and dynamic treatment effect. The first untreated outcome follows a two-way fixed-effects model. The second adds two interactive latent factors with different mean loadings for treated and control units.


Code
import crabbymetrics as cm
import pandas as pd
import pyfixest as pf

application_adoption = 20
application_dimensions = core.PanelDimensions(n_units=120, n_periods=30)
application_assignment = primitives.RandomizedSingleCohortAssignment(
    n_treated=24,
    adoption_period=application_adoption,
)
application_effect = primitives.LinearRampEffect(slope=0.2)

additive_application = core.PanelSimulator(
    name="additive_twfe_application",
    dimensions=application_dimensions,
    assignment=application_assignment,
    outcome_model=primitives.TwoWayFixedEffectsOutcome(
        unit_effect_scale=1.0,
        time_effect_scale=0.5,
        noise_scale=0.75,
    ),
    effect_model=application_effect,
).simulate(seed=42)

interactive_application = core.PanelSimulator(
    name="interactive_factor_application",
    dimensions=application_dimensions,
    assignment=application_assignment,
    outcome_model=primitives.SumOutcomeModel(
        models=(
            primitives.TwoWayFixedEffectsOutcome(
                unit_effect_scale=1.0,
                time_effect_scale=0.0,
                noise_scale=0.0,
            ),
            primitives.LowRankFactorOutcome(
                rank=2,
                control_loading_mean=-0.1,
                treated_loading_mean=0.1,
                noise_scale=0.75,
            ),
        )
    ),
    effect_model=application_effect,
).simulate(seed=42)



9.1 PyFixest two-way fixed effects
PyFixest consumes the long representation. The event-study regression omits event time \(-1\), and the static regression reports an ATT summary. Standard errors are clustered by unit.


Code
def fit_pyfixest(draw):
    frame = pd.DataFrame(dict(draw.as_long_dict()))
    frame["ever_treated"] = np.repeat(
        draw.ever_treated,
        draw.n_periods,
    ).astype(int)
    event_fit = pf.feols(
        f"outcome ~ i(time, ever_treated, ref={application_adoption - 1})"
        " | unit + time",
        data=frame,
        vcov={"CRV1": "unit"},
    )
    att_fit = pf.feols(
        "outcome ~ treatment | unit + time",
        data=frame,
        vcov={"CRV1": "unit"},
    )

    event = event_fit.tidy().reset_index()
    term_column = event.columns[0]
    event["period"] = (
        event[term_column]
        .astype(str)
        .str.extract(r"time::(-?\d+)")[0]
        .astype(int)
    )
    event["event_time"] = event["period"] - application_adoption
    event = event.rename(
        columns={
            "Estimate": "estimate",
            "2.5%": "lower",
            "97.5%": "upper",
        }
    )
    event = pd.concat(
        [
            event[["event_time", "estimate", "lower", "upper"]],
            pd.DataFrame(
                {
                    "event_time": [-1],
                    "estimate": [0.0],
                    "lower": [0.0],
                    "upper": [0.0],
                }
            ),
        ],
        ignore_index=True,
    ).sort_values("event_time")
    att_row = att_fit.tidy().loc["treatment"]
    return {
        "event": event,
        "att": float(att_row["Estimate"]),
        "att_se": float(att_row["Std. Error"]),
    }




9.2 crabbymetrics matrix completion
MatrixCompletion consumes the native unit-by-period arrays. It estimates the missing treated counterfactual from the untreated cells and returns an ATT and weighted event-study path.


Code
def fit_matrix_completion(draw):
    model = cm.MatrixCompletion(
        lambda_fraction=0.25,
        max_iterations=2_000,
        tolerance=1e-7,
        svd_seed=1,
    )
    model.fit(
        draw.outcome.copy(),
        draw.treatment.copy(),
    )
    summary = model.summary()
    return {
        "event": pd.DataFrame(summary["event_study"]["weighted"]),
        "att": float(summary["att"]),
    }




9.3 crabbymetrics interactive fixed effects
InteractiveFixedEffects is a factor decomposition, not a treatment-effect estimator. Here it fits the complete donor panel. Treated-unit loadings are estimated only from pre-treatment outcomes, then extrapolated over the fitted donor factors.


Code
def fit_interactive_fixed_effects(draw, *, rank):
    outcome, _ = draw.as_arrays(copy=True)
    donors = draw.control_units
    treated = draw.treated_units
    adoption = int(np.unique(draw.adoption_times[treated]).item())

    model = cm.InteractiveFixedEffects(
        rank=rank,
        force=3,
        factor_seed=1,
    )
    model.fit(outcome[donors].T)
    decomposition = model.summary()
    factors = np.asarray(decomposition["factor"])
    time_effects = np.asarray(decomposition["xi"])

    pre_design = np.column_stack(
        [np.ones(adoption), factors[:adoption]],
    )
    full_design = np.column_stack(
        [np.ones(draw.n_periods), factors],
    )
    treated_coefficients = np.linalg.lstsq(
        pre_design,
        outcome[treated, :adoption].T - time_effects[:adoption, None],
        rcond=None,
    )[0]
    counterfactual = (
        time_effects[:, None] + full_design @ treated_coefficients
    ).T
    estimated_effect = outcome[treated] - counterfactual
    return {
        "event": pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "event_time": np.arange(draw.n_periods) - adoption,
                "estimate": estimated_effect.mean(axis=0),
            }
        ),
        "att": float(estimated_effect[:, adoption:].mean()),
    }




9.4 Compare the estimates
The simulation supplies the rank used by interactive fixed effects. This example does not estimate the rank.

application_results = {}
for label, draw, rank in (
    ("Additive 2WFE", additive_application, 0),
    ("Interactive factors", interactive_application, 2),
):
    application_results[label] = {
        "draw": draw,
        "pyfixest": fit_pyfixest(draw),
        "matrix_completion": fit_matrix_completion(draw),
        "interactive_fixed_effects": fit_interactive_fixed_effects(
            draw,
            rank=rank,
        ),
    }

pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "design": label,
            "true ATT": result["draw"].true_att,

            "crabbymetrics IFE": result["interactive_fixed_effects"]["att"],

Figure 2: PyFixest and crabbymetrics applied to additive and interactive-factor panels with known treatment effects.





For the additive panel, 2WFE is correctly specified. For the interactive panel, the fixed-effects regression omits the latent factors. Matrix completion and the donor-factor estimate use low-rank structure instead. These are illustrative seeded results, not an estimator ranking: matrix completion uses its default penalty fraction, IFE is given the design rank, and only the PyFixest curve includes sampling uncertainty.

title: Treatment assignment
text:
2 Common simulation components
The examples below share the same features, untreated outcomes, and treatment effects. Only assignment changes.


Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from pypanelsim import core, primitives

dimensions = core.PanelDimensions(n_units=240, n_periods=48)
features = primitives.GaussianUnitFeatures(
    n_observables=2,
    n_unobservables=1,
)
outcome = primitives.SumOutcomeModel(
    models=(
        primitives.TwoWayFixedEffectsOutcome(noise_scale=0.4),
        primitives.LinearFeatureOutcome(
            level_coefficients=(1.0, -0.5),
            trend_coefficients=(0.0, 0.0),
            source="observables",
        ),
        primitives.LinearFeatureOutcome(
            level_coefficients=(0.8,),
            trend_coefficients=(0.0,),
            source="unobservables",
        ),
    )
)
effect = primitives.LinearRampEffect(slope=0.12)

def make_simulator(name, assignment):
    return core.PanelSimulator(
        name=name,
        dimensions=dimensions,
        feature_model=features,
        assignment=assignment,
        outcome_model=outcome,
        effect_model=effect,
    )

text:
4 Selection with a binary logit
For unit \(i\), BinaryLogitAssignment uses
\[
P(A_i=1 \mid X_i,U_i)
= \operatorname{logit}^{-1}
\left(\alpha + X_i'\beta + U_i'\gamma\right).
\]
Here \(X_i\) is observable to the estimator and \(U_i\) is latent.


Code
selected = make_simulator(
    "selected_single_cohort",
    primitives.BinaryLogitAssignment(
        adoption_period=30,
        intercept=-0.3,
        observable_coefficients=(0.8, -0.4),
        unobservable_coefficients=(0.9,),
    ),
).simulate(seed=42)

print(selected.treated_units.size)
print(selected.unit_covariate_names)


111
('x1', 'x2')


The same latent feature affects untreated outcomes and assignment. The design therefore has unobserved selection by construction.

text:
7 Unit-time effect heterogeneity
An effect callable receives the same observed, latent, and time features as the other components. It returns the potential effect for every cell. The simulator sets the realized effect to zero outside treated cells.


Code
heterogeneous_simulator = core.PanelSimulator(
    name="heterogeneous_effects",
    dimensions=dimensions,
    feature_model=features,
    time_feature_model=primitives.GaussianTimeFeatures(1),
    assignment=primitives.RandomizedSingleCohortAssignment(
        n_treated=80,
        adoption_period=30,
    ),
    outcome_model=outcome,
    effect_model=lambda context: (
        (
            1.0
            + 0.45 * context.observables[:, 0]
            - 0.30 * context.observables[:, 1]
            + 0.80 * context.unobservables[:, 0]
        )[:, None]
        * (1.0 + 0.30 * context.time_features[:, 0])[None, :]
    ),
)
heterogeneous_panel = heterogeneous_simulator.simulate(seed=42)

text: These simulations follow Large Scale Longitudinal Experiments by Apoorva Lal, Alexander Fischer, and Matthew Wardrop, with public code. The simulations test regression compression under several panel structures; storage and distributed estimation are outside this example.

title: Large panels and compressed regressions
text:
1 Scientific question
Suppose raw longitudinal data are too large to centralize. A site can transmit small regression summaries instead. A simulation should test whether those summaries preserve the treatment-effect information under trends, serial dependence, and heterogeneous effects.

import numpy as np

from pypanelsim import designs

title: Large panels and compressed regressions
text:
2 Main panel design
The untreated outcome contains unit effects, time effects, unit-specific linear trends, and AR(1) error. One cohort adopts treatment. The effect path can be concave or another configured profile, with optional unit heterogeneity.

title: Large panels and compressed regressions
text:
3 A minimal compressed summary
For a regression \(y=X\beta+u\), a site can summarize its data with \(X'X\), \(X'y\), \(y'y\), and the observation count. Sites can add these terms without sharing rows.
The example below uses treatment, a post indicator, and their interaction. It is deliberately small; an applied design would add its required fixed-effect or basis representation.


Code
columns = panel.as_long_dict()
y = columns["outcome"]

post = (columns["time"] >= config.adoption_period).astype(float)
treated_unit = np.repeat(panel.ever_treated.astype(float), panel.n_periods)
x = np.column_stack(
    (
        np.ones(y.size),
        treated_unit,
        post,
        treated_unit * post,
    )
)

summary = {
    "n": y.size,
    "xtx": x.T @ x,
    "xty": x.T @ y,
    "yty": float(y @ y),
}

beta_from_summary = np.linalg.solve(summary["xtx"], summary["xty"])
beta_from_rows = np.linalg.lstsq(x, y, rcond=None)[0]

print(np.allclose(beta_from_summary, beta_from_rows))
print(np.round(beta_from_summary, 3))


True
[ 0.13   0.133 -0.591  0.261]


This equality is algebraic for the stated regression. It does not show that the interaction coefficient equals the desired dynamic-effect estimand. Compression and causal identification are separate questions.

title: Large panels and compressed regressions
text:
4 Combine summaries across sites


Code
site_ids = np.array_split(np.arange(panel.n_units), 4)
site_summaries = []

for site_units in site_ids:
    rows = np.isin(columns["unit"], site_units)
    x_site = x[rows]
    y_site = y[rows]
    site_summaries.append((x_site.T @ x_site, x_site.T @ y_site))

pooled_xtx = sum(item[0] for item in site_summaries)
pooled_xty = sum(item[1] for item in site_summaries)
pooled_beta = np.linalg.solve(pooled_xtx, pooled_xty)

print(np.allclose(pooled_beta, beta_from_rows))


True


The partition has no effect because the summaries are additive.

title: Large panels and compressed regressions
text:
6 What to report
A compression experiment should report both layers:

the causal design: assignment, untreated outcomes, potential effects, and target;
the transmitted summary: regressors, sufficient statistics, grouping, and numeric precision.

A small communication cost is not useful if the summary corresponds to the wrong regression or the regression corresponds to the wrong causal target.

title: Research designs
text:
2 Baker dynamic effects
Baker’s design shows why a two-way fixed-effects coefficient can differ from the average effect when cohorts adopt at different times and their effects grow at different rates. States enter one of three cohorts, untreated outcomes contain state and year effects, and each cohort has its own linear effect path. title: Balancing validation snapshot
text:
Stored R and Python results provide a cross-language check for augmented balancing experiments. Everything shown on this page is in the repository; the original research directories are not required.
The estimator is provided by crabbymetrics. The related paper is Augmented Balancing Estimators of the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated in Cross-Sectional and Panel Designs.

title: Balancing validation snapshot
text:
1 Validation question
The check asks whether the Python simulation and estimator pipeline gives Monte Carlo RMSE values consistent with an earlier R reference grid.
The two languages did not use matched random draws. Therefore, equality cell by cell is not the correct criterion. For cell \(j\), compare
\[
Z_j=
\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{RMSE}}_{P,j}-
      \widehat{\mathrm{RMSE}}_{R,j}}
{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{MCSE}}_{P,j}^2+
       \widehat{\mathrm{MCSE}}_{R,j}^2}}.
\]
Values within a few combined Monte Carlo standard errors are consistent with simulation noise.

title: How simulation works
text:
A PanelSimulator evaluates components in this order:

The unit-feature model draws observed and latent features.
The assignment model draws the binary treatment matrix.
The time-feature model draws shared time features, if present.
The outcome model draws untreated outcomes.
The effect model draws potential effects for every cell and realized effects.
The simulator validates and freezes the result.

Each step can use results from earlier steps. For example, an outcome model can use both unit features and treatment timing, which permits selection on untreated trends. The model definition makes that dependence explicit.

title: How simulation works
text:
3 Write a custom component
Each component satisfies a small protocol:

UnitFeatureModel.generate(dimensions, rng) returns a UnitFeatureDraw.
AssignmentModel.assign(context, rng) returns a ComponentDraw.
TimeFeatureModel.generate(dimensions, rng) returns a TimeFeatureDraw.
OutcomeModel.generate(context, rng) returns untreated outcomes.
EffectModel.generate(context, rng) returns realized effects.

The protocols are structural. A custom dataclass does not need to inherit from a package base class. It only needs the correct method and return type.

title: How simulation works
text:
4 Matrix conventions
All panel matrices use (unit, time) order. For \(N\) units and \(T\) periods, each matrix has shape \(N \times T\).



Matrix
Definition




outcome
observed outcome \(Y\)


treatment
binary assignment \(D\)


untreated_outcome
untreated potential outcome \(Y(0)\)


effect_surface
effect if treated, \(\tau\)


treatment_effect
realized effect \(D \odot \tau\)



The simulator enforces
\[
Y = Y(0) + D \odot \tau.
\]
It rejects non-finite values, mismatched shapes, non-binary treatment, a realized effect outside treated cells, and a broken causal identity.

title: Composite panel benchmark
text: The composite family is a package benchmark. It is not a reproduction of a published paper. Its purpose is to test an estimator when several familiar untreated-outcome structures are present at once.

title: Composite panel benchmark
text:
1 Outcome decomposition
The untreated outcome is a weighted sum of four components:
\[
Y(0)
=w_FY_F+w_TY_T+w_SY_S+w_AY_A+\varepsilon,
\]
where \(Y_F\) is a low-rank factor component, \(Y_T\) is a persistent time-series component, \(Y_S\) has sparse synthetic-control donor structure, and \(Y_A\) is an additive two-way fixed-effects component.
The weights are explicit configuration fields. They need not sum to one, but a sum of one makes their relative scale easier to interpret.

title: Support-aware event studies
text: The partial-pooling family adapts an ongoing working-paper design for pooling across staggered-adoption cohorts. Names and details may change with that work.

title: Support-aware event studies
text:
1 Scientific question
An event-study estimator faces two distinct problems:

Cohorts can have different effect paths.
A cohort-event comparison can fall outside the observed calendar.

Pooling can reduce variance when cohort paths are similar. It can add bias when they differ. No amount of pooling creates a missing calendar-time observation.

title: Support-aware event studies

7 Define the event-time target
At a fixed event time, different cohorts can contribute because of calendar support. The target population therefore changes with event time.


Code

    event_times=range(-4, 13),
    weighting="cohort_size",
)
equal_cohort = panel.truth.event_study(
    event_times=range(-4, 13),
    weighting="equal_cohort",
)

for index in range(0, len(size_weighted["event_time"]), 4):
    print(
        int(size_weighted["event_time"][index]),
        round(float(size_weighted["effect"][index]), 3),
        round(float(equal_cohort["effect"][index]), 3),
        int(size_weighted["supported_cohorts"][index]),

title: Support-aware event studies
text:
8 A clean Monte Carlo grid
A useful grid crosses pooling structure with noise and sample size:
design_names = (
    "complete_homogeneity",
    "cohort_only_blocks",
    "tensor_blocks",
    "no_pool_signed_paths",
)
noise_scales = (0.5, 1.0, 2.0)
unit_counts = (600, 1200, 2400)
Hold the event-time target and support rule fixed across this grid. Then changes in bias or coverage can be attributed to the estimator’s pooling decision, rather than to a silent change in the estimand.

title: Baker’s dynamic-effects example
text:
3 The TWFE coefficient
For a balanced panel, residualize a matrix against unit and time fixed effects by double demeaning:
\[
\widetilde Z_{it}
=Z_{it}-\bar Z_{i\cdot}-\bar Z_{\cdot t}+\bar Z_{\cdot\cdot}.
\]
The coefficient from \(Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\gamma_t+\beta D_{it}+u_{it}\) is then
\[
\widehat\beta
=\frac{\sum_{it}\widetilde D_{it}\widetilde Y_{it}}
{\sum_{it}\widetilde D_{it}^2}.
\]


Code
def double_demean(values):
    return (
        values
        - values.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        - values.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
        + values.mean()
    )

d_tilde = double_demean(panel.treatment)
y_tilde = double_demean(panel.outcome)
twfe = float(np.sum(d_tilde * y_tilde) / np.sum(d_tilde**2))

print("TWFE coefficient:", round(twfe, 4))
print("true treated-cell ATT:", round(panel.true_att, 4))
print("difference:", round(twfe - panel.true_att, 4))


TWFE coefficient: -0.2034
true treated-cell ATT: 0.8901
difference: -1.0935


The difference is not a software error. The regression coefficient weights cells by residualized treatment. With staggered adoption, already-treated cohorts can act as comparisons for later cohorts. Dynamic and cohort-varying effects then enter with weights that do not match treated-cell ATT weights.

text:
6 What this design does not prove
One simulation does not show that TWFE always fails. It shows a case where its coefficient and a common ATT target differ. Change effect slopes, cohort sizes, timing, and noise across replications before making a performance claim about an estimator.
